caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 124 of 2010
lawyer:
Quamrul Islam Siddique, Advocate instructed by Md. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioner 
Shaheed Alam, Senior Advocate instructed by Syed Mahbubar Rahman, Advocate-on-Record ------- For Respondent No.2 
For Respondent No. 1 ------- None represented.
parties:
Md. Hossain Ahmed ------ Petitioner.
VS
Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation and another ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J: In this, petition for leave to appeal the judgment debtor-petitioner has called in question the propriety of the judgment and order dated the 8th day of November, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1080 of 2009 discharging the Rule ratifying the judgment and order dated 26.02.2009 passed by the learned District Judge, Jessore in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 16 of 2007. 

 2. Facts necessary for disposal of this leave petition, in short, are that respondent No.1, Bangladesh House Finance Corporation instituted Miscellaneous Case No.16 of 1991 before the Artha Rin Adalat at Jessore under the provision of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 (P.O. No.7 of 1973) against the petitioner for realization of  an amount of TK. 8,95,690.25 as on 31.12.1998 alone with interest, by selling the land along with the  building standing thereon as fully described in the schedule to the application. The miscellaneous case was allowed ex-parte on 06.06.1992 in preliminary form directing the judgment-debtor-petitioner to pay the decretal amount within 3(three) Months, in default, to realize the decretal amount by selling the properties as described in the schedule to the application. As the judgment-debtor did not pay the decretal amount the decree-holder levied Money Execution Case No.129 of 1996 in the same Artha Rin Adalat for realization of the decretal amount. During pendency of the execution case the judgment-debtor-petitioner sold the mortgaged property to respondent No.2, namely, Kamrunnahar Nazma by a registered sale deed dated 07.08.2006. It further appears that at the direction of the execution Court, respondent No. 2 deposited a sum of TK. 12,38,578.49 in favour of decree-holder i.e. House Building Finance Corporation (respondent No. 2 herein) and she was also impleaded in the execution case as judgment-debtor No. 2. On deposit of the said decretal amount by respondent No. 2, the executing Court disposed of the execution case on full satisfaction. Thereafter, the decree-holder-respondent No.1 filed an application before the execution Court on 25.01.2007 for delivery of possession of the mortgaged property in favour of respondent No. 2 by evicting the original judgment-debtor i.e. the present' petitioner. The executing Court rejected the prayer by its order dated 13.02.2007 on the view that since the execution case was disposed of on full satisfaction the application was incompetent. 

 3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said order of the executing Court, respondent No. 1 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 16 of 2007 before the District Judge, Jessore. The learned District Judge who heard the miscellaneous appeal, by his order dated 26.02.2009 allowed the same directing the executing Court to pass necessary order as per law so that possession of the mortgaged property might be delivered in favour of respondent No. 2. 

 4. Against the order of the learned District Judge, the original judgment-debtor-petitioner filed Civil Revision No.1080 of 2009 before the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division which heard the revision though found that miscellaneous appeal in question filed before the District Judge was incompetent, yet it "ratified" the order passed by the District Judge invoking the inherent power of the Court as mandated in section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code), hence, this petition for leave to appeal before this Division. 

 5. Mr. Quamrul Islam Siddique, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioner, submits that since the miscellaneous, appeal before the District Judge was not maintainable, the High Court Division erred in law in maintaining the order passed by the District Judge by ratifying the same invoking the inherent power of the Court under section 151 of the Code. Mr. Siddique further submits that the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider that respondent No.2 who was subsequently impleaded in the execution case as a judgment-debtor, had some other obligations to the petitioner which she did not fulfill, so, if the delivery of possession of the mortgaged property is given to her as directed by the appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court Division by way of ratification, the petitioner would be left with no remedy against her. Mr. Siddique lastly submits that since the execution case in question was disposed of on full satisfaction, no order for delivery of possession of the mortgaged property to respondent No.2 could be passed and remedy of the respondent to get possession of the mortgaged properly, if at all, was by a separate proceeding, but the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider this legal aspect of the case and thus erred in law in passing the impugned order. On the above submissions, Mr. Siddique prayed for granting leave to the petitioner to appeal to this Division. 

 7. From the facts stated herein before, it is clear that the present-petitioner who was the original judgment-debtor in the execution case in question sold the mortgaged property to respondent No. 2 during the pendency of the execution case. Not only that at the order of the executing Court respondent No. 2 also paid TK. 12,38,578.49 in favour of the decree-holder but the execution case was dismissed of on full satisfaction without caring to deliver possession of the mortgaged property to her. The petitioner being the judgment-debtor and having sold the mortgaged property to respondent No.2 it was his moral and legal obligation to take step to deliver possession of the sold property to her, moreso, when she paid the entire dues of the House Building Finance Corporation and thus redeemed the mortgaged property, but he took no step to that end. It is indeed respondent No.1, the decree-holder who filed the application before the executing Court to deliver possession of the mortgaged property to respondent No. 2, but that is being opposed by the petitioner. The attempt made by the petitioner in opposing the prayer for delivering possession of the mortgaged property to respondent No. 2 appears to as not bonafide and also shocking to conscience. Since the execution case in question was disposed of on payment of the decretal amount by respondent No. 2 without deity eying possession of the mortgaged property to her, the decree-holder rightly filed the application for the purpose. It is necessary to state that the decree was passed by the Artha Rin Adalat in preliminary form in favour of the decree-holder for selling the mortgaged property. We have given our anxious thought over the matter as to whether, in the facts and circumstances of the case stated hereinbefore, there was any other provision either in the Code or in the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 to take effective step to cause delivery of possession of the mortgaged property to respondent No. 2, but we could not lay our hand on any provision other than section 151 of the Code. In the above backdrop of facts, we find no other alternative but to approve the innovative approach of the High Court Division in ratifying the order of the appellate Court passed in the miscellaneous appeal. Had the High Court Division not ratified the order passed in the miscellaneous appeal invoking the inherent power of the Court as mandated in section 151 of the Code, respondent No. 2 would have been thrown on the street and would have never got possession of the mortgaged property though she had to pay the price for the same twice, first to the original judgment-debtor and then to be decree-holder in the execution case.
